analysis.title: Investment Weekly, 30 October 2026
key_insights: Chart of the week: the Fed left the funds rate unchanged in October. HSBC says restrictive policy and gradual further tightening are still needed against sticky inflation, with oil's renewed rise adding upside inflation risk.
The US economy is K-shaped. Policy is too accommodative for sectors tied to the AI boom and too tight for industries further from it or competing with tech for capital.

US large caps and small caps have split since late summer. The S&P 500 is supported by megacap earnings despite AI capex worries, while the rate-sensitive Russell 2000 has fallen as markets price more Fed tightening.

Markets price three more Fed hikes, implying a peak funds rate above 4.50% in 2027. HSBC expects only two more hikes because higher bond yields are already cooling growth and oil may moderate in line with the futures curve.
A less hawkish Fed outcome should help unwind the K-shaped divergence and bring a modest softening in the US dollar. HSBC expects the broadening-out trade to stay alive in 2027.

Market Spotlight: with mainstream corporate bond spreads near the tight end of their historical range, HSBC sees the best value in securitised credit. Senior AAA and single-A tranches are protected by junior tranches that absorb defaults first, and most pay floating rates, so duration risk is near zero.
Securitised credit pays wider spreads than corporate bonds because of structural complexity and lower liquidity. HSBC says this makes research, security selection and manager skill essential.

US midterms: since 1950, US equity performance has consistently accelerated in the year after midterm elections. HSBC cautions that correlation is not causation and that many such rallies coincided with strong secular tailwinds. It also says another 20% gain is a tall order after recent strength.

A divided government after the midterms would reduce the risk of sweeping fiscal or legislative surprises, though the administration might lean more on executive actions and trade policy. HSBC sees clearing the midterms as a potential tailwind.

Brazil: Lula's unexpected re-election triggered a sharp repricing of Brazilian assets. Opposition gains in Congress point to legislative gridlock and a persistently elevated fiscal risk premium. HSBC's EM debt team still thinks rates are unsustainably high and likely to fall over the coming year.
HSBC also sees Brazilian equities as offering bargain valuations and large dividend yields, and says AI-driven commodity demand and high oil prices play to Brazil's strengths.

UK Budget: Chancellor Healey's first Budget was cautious and the market reaction was muted. Consolidation relies mainly on tax increases while revenues are already at post-WWII highs as a share of GDP, which leaves slippage risk.

The BoE is expected to raise rates toward 4.50% in H1 2027, which should keep 10-year gilt yields elevated near term. HSBC still sees G7-topping gilt yields as attractive income and expects a modest decline in yields over 12 months.

House view framing is 'two shocks and a boom': an oil-driven inflation shock from the Middle East conflict, a mildly disinflationary 'China shock 2.0' from tech and green-energy exports, and the US AI investment boom. HSBC expects episodic volatility and a cautiously pro-risk stance.

House view on duration: modest curve steepening, with the Fed delivering less tightening than priced. On 10-year Treasuries, yields should stay range-bound near term with modest downward pressure later. On credit, tight spreads argue for a quality bias with investment grade as a credible bond substitute and selectivity in high yield.

House view on equities and EM: DM equities should see 'broadening out 2.0' from AI spillovers, with elevated oil and higher-for-longer rates as risks. EM equities and EM hard-currency bonds are described as constructive, helped by earnings upgrades and valuations.

Weekly market moves: global equities rose, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq gained, and the Russell 2000 outperformed. US Treasury yields declined broadly. The Bovespa fell 17.5% in the week and the Brazilian real lost 8.1% against the dollar after the election.
Commodities: Brent was 116.4 and WTI 103.4, up 18.8% and 16.9% over one month. Gold was 3,988, down 4.1% over the month and 7.7% year to date.
earnings_insights: Per the calendar commentary, about 45% of Q3 US earnings were released as of the report. The weakest areas are real estate and consumer discretionary. The text also gives '2026 EPS around 35%' but the context is truncated in the document.
Megacap earnings are described as 'bumper' and supporting the S&P 500, with lingering concerns over AI capex plans. Tech heavyweights were mixed this week.
South Korea's Kospi traded higher this week amid earnings releases from semiconductor heavyweights.

risk_factors: Sticky inflation and a renewed rise in oil prices could force more Fed tightening than HSBC expects.
AI capex concerns despite strong megacap earnings.
A persistently elevated oil price and higher-for-longer rates could weigh on growth.
Tight credit spreads in global credit, high yield and Asia credit leave limited compensation for downside risks.

UK fiscal slippage, since consolidation relies heavily on tax increases and revenues are already at post-WWII highs as a share of GDP.
Geopolitical shocks and supply chain disruption in Asia.
Global trade fragmentation as a challenge for EM.
charts_described: Chart of the week plots the S&P 500 (left axis) against the Russell 2000 (right axis) from January to October 2026, with the two indices splitting into a K-shape since late summer.
A chart of the S&P 500 around midterm elections since 1950 shows the mean path against the current electoral cycle, annotated with 'Liberation Day' and 'Iran'.
A chart of Brazil 10-year government bond yields and USD/BRL from 2024 to 2026 carries the annotations 'rising fiscal concerns' and 'AI commodity boom and EM rally'.
A chart of UK public sector current receipts versus total managed expenditure as a share of GDP carries OBR forecasts.
vol_and_positioning: HSBC expects episodic volatility in a confusing macro landscape of two shocks and a boom.
Brazil's election sell-off was violent, with the Bovespa down 17.5% in a week and the real down 8.1%.
Hedge funds, especially macro and CTA strategies, are described as good diversifiers in elevated inflation, sharp volatility upticks and periods of positive stock-bond correlation.
geopolitical: Middle East conflict is pushing oil prices higher and is the main inflationary shock in the house view.

Brazil's second-round presidential election on 25 October produced an unexpected Lula victory, triggering a sharp sell-off in Brazilian assets. Opposition gains in Congress point to legislative gridlock.
US midterm elections on 3 November. The latest polls suggest Democrats will gain a majority in both the House and the Senate.
'Liberation Day' tariffs and Iran are cited as past political events that rattled market sentiment.
'China shock 2.0' from China's surging tech and green energy exports is described as mildly disinflationary, with global trade fragmentation a challenge for EM.
Geopolitical tensions are cited as a supply chain disruption risk for Asian markets.

tension_points.bull_case: HSBC argues the Fed is near the limit of useful restrictiveness. The jump in bond yields is already cooling growth and oil may moderate in line with the futures curve, so two more hikes rather than three would be enough, helping unwind the K-shaped market divergence.
tension_points.bear_case: Inflation is sticky and oil's renewed rise heightens upside inflation risk. The market prices three more hikes and a peak funds rate above 4.50% in 2027, which keeps pressure on the rate-sensitive Russell 2000.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Oil failing to moderate in line with the futures curve, which the report treats as a reasonable but not certain outcome.

tension_points.bull_case: After the violent sell-off, HSBC's EM debt team thinks rates are unsustainably high and likely to fall. Equities offer bargain valuations and large dividend yields, and AI-driven commodity demand and high oil prices suit Brazil.
tension_points.bear_case: Opposition gains in Congress point to legislative gridlock that complicates fiscal credibility and keeps the fiscal risk premium elevated.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Pragmatic compromise with centrist lawmakers failing to unlock fiscal consolidation and key economic appointments.

tension_points.bull_case: G7-topping yields provide attractive income, and subdued UK growth plus a possible moderation in oil prices in 2027 should allow a modest decline in yields over 12 months.
tension_points.bear_case: Fiscal consolidation relies heavily on tax increases with revenues already at post-WWII highs, backloaded consolidation and persistent inflation concerns, with the BoE expected to hike, keep yields elevated near term.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Cyclical deterioration knocking the upwardly revised 2028-30 OBR GDP forecasts off course, which would raise slippage risk.
